newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo JAT eyes 1.5 mln passengers in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Yugo JAT eyes 1.5 mln passengers in 1997.

text.p: Yugoslav airlines Jugoslovenski aerotransport (JAT) said on Tuesday it expects to carry 1.5 million passengers in 1997 and expand flights to the United States, Canada and Middle East in its winter timetable.

"JAT plans to carry 1.5 million passengers in 1997 on domestic, international and intercontinental flights. If we do not resume intercontinental flights, we shall have to increase the number of passengers on European destinations," JAT general manager Zika Petrovic told Reuters in an interview.
"Without intercontinental flights, we'll have 1.3 to 1.35 million passengers."
Petrovic saw JAT carrying three million people and 50,000 tonnes of cargo by the year 2000.

Yugoslav flag carrier submitted requests to the U.S. and Canadian aviation authorities for resumption of flights earlier this year. Canada is expected to deliver its answer for an ABC charter by the end of June or beginning of July.

"We are determined to reopen regular flights and our requests to the American and Canadian authorities are clear. Their response is of political nature and denies a right to more than 300,000 Yugo-Americans to directly fly to Yugoslavia.
"But the outer wall of sanctions in air transport does not mean much because people fly anyway and come to Belgrade via London, Amsterdam," Petrovic said.

In 1996, JAT carried 900,000 instead of planned one million passengers partly because the company was still banned from flying to the U.S. and Canada and because of a three-month political turmoil in Serbia.
"We had a very problematic political life at the end of 1996. Not only JAT but other airlines also recorded a 25-30 percent decline in their activities," he said.
JAT will launch direct flights to some Greek islands, Spanish holiday resorts and other tourist destinations during the summer season and will introduce flights to Bratislava.

"We are negotiating with several Slovak companies to link Bratislava with Western Europe. JAT would fly from Belgrade to Bratislava and from there together with the local partner to London, Zurich, Frankfurt," Petrovic said.
Winter timetable was planned to include new flights to Cairo, Beirut, Amman and Damascus while a programme of flights to Abu Dhabi and Dubai was in preparation.
JAT ended 1996 with $122 million income and plans to raise income to $216 million in 1997.

"Our aim is profit, but our performance is handicapped because the economy still has limits, insufficient business ties with the world, no membership in international financial and trade bodies. And JAT is expected to meet all criteria and compete with 12 foreign airlines in Belgrade," Petrovic said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
